findings.description: The python half of release_body_identical coerces three non-conforming read-backs into a comparable body instead of exiting non-zero. (a) A non-object JSON document (array, string, number, null) yields body None, then '' (lines 1199-1201), so python prints `differ N 0`, or `equal` when the sent notes are empty; the refusal then depends solely on the later jq identity step erroring on `.id` (unreadable) or failing the id term. (b) A dict with `body: null` is likewise treated as '' and compares equal to empty notes, where the previous `.body == $body` jq test refused null. (c) `body.encode('utf-8', 'surrogateescape')` (line 1204) maps lone surrogates U+DC80..U+DCFF in the read-back JSON onto raw bytes 0x80..0xFF, so a read-back body spelled `"\udcc3\udca9"` compares equal to a sent body containing `é`. GitHub's API cannot return lone surrogates today, and the jq step covers (a), so none of this is exploitable; it is a tolerance wider than the single caret rewrite the helper is documented to accept, and it leans on a second guard that a later jq edit (e.g. `.id?`) would silently remove.
findings.failure_mode: A read-back that is not a release object, or that carries lone surrogates, is normalised into a comparable body by python rather than refused there; correctness of the refusal rests on the separate jq identity check rather than on the helper that owns the body comparison.
findings.suggested_fix: In the python program: `if not isinstance(rb, dict): raise SystemExit('read-back is not an object')`; treat `body is None` the same way as a non-string (refuse) unless the sent notes are also empty, or compare against b'' only when `rb.get('body') in ('', None)` AND `sent == b''`; encode with `'strict'` so lone surrogates raise UnicodeEncodeError and refuse. Add a bats case for an array read-back and one for a `\udc80` body to pin the behaviour.
findings.failure_scenario: A read-back that is not a release object, or that carries lone surrogates, is normalised into a comparable body by python rather than refused there; correctness of the refusal rests on the separate jq identity check rather than on the helper that owns the body comparison.

findings.description: The helper creates `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/release-body.XXXXXX/` (mode 0700, unpredictable name, so no symlink or pre-placement attack is possible from another user) and removes it with `rm -rf` only on the normal return path. There is no `trap ... RETURN/EXIT/INT/TERM`, so SIGKILL, SIGTERM from the CI runner, or a `set -e` abort inside the helper leaves `sent` (the full release notes) and `readback` (the full GitHub release JSON) on disk. The caller's `body_err` file (line 1304) has the same lifecycle gap. Contents are public release text and the directory is owner-only, so exposure is nil on a shared sticky /tmp; this is hygiene, not disclosure.
findings.failure_mode: Abrupt termination of the orchestrator leaves per-run temp files containing the release body and read-back JSON under TMPDIR indefinitely.
findings.suggested_fix: Install `trap 'rm -rf "$dir"' RETURN` immediately after the successful `mktemp -d` (bash supports RETURN traps in functions), or register the directory in a script-level cleanup list consumed by an EXIT trap; do the same for `$body_err`. SIGKILL cannot be trapped, so optionally sweep `release-body.*` older than a day at script start.
findings.failure_scenario: Abrupt termination of the orchestrator leaves per-run temp files containing the release body and read-back JSON under TMPDIR indefinitely.

findings.description: `body_err=$(mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/release-body-err.XXXXXX")` has no `|| ...` branch. The surrounding comment says the script runs under `set -e`; a failing command substitution in a plain assignment terminates the shell. At this point the release POST has already succeeded (lines 1288-1292), so an ENOSPC or unwritable TMPDIR here aborts the orchestrator with the release phase still recorded as in_progress and no `fail_phase` receipt explaining why. Nothing downstream (ledger push, notify) runs, so it is fail-closed in effect, but the state receipt the sprint is explicitly trying to make explanatory is not written. Not exploitable; a robustness gap in the new fail-closed wrapper.
findings.failure_mode: mktemp failure after the release has been created exits the script without a recorded phase failure, leaving the state file inconsistent with GitHub.
findings.suggested_fix: `body_err=$(mktemp ...) || { fail_phase release "Release body comparison failed: cannot create stderr capture file; release not verified"; return 1; }`. Alternatively capture python's stderr into a variable via process substitution or `2>&1 >/dev/null` inside the helper so no second temp file is needed.
findings.failure_scenario: mktemp failure after the release has been created exits the script without a recorded phase failure, leaving the state file inconsistent with GitHub.

findings.cross_file_justification: The orchestrator's new helper (post-merge-orchestrator.sh:1193) and caller (:1304) write under `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}`; the new bats cases invoke them via `publish` and via direct `source`, so the test run writes outside `$CASE_DIR` unless the harness exports TMPDIR.
findings.description: Reviewer concern 6 asks whether anything is written outside the case directory. The explicit test artefacts (`$CASE_DIR/big.txt`, `$CASE_DIR/big-rb.json`, `${GH_LOG}.release`, `$PROJECT_ROOT/.claude/scripts/source-orchestrator.sh`) stay inside the per-case tree. However every new case that reaches the release phase or calls `release_body_identical` directly causes the code under test to create `release-body.XXXXXX/` and `release-body-err.XXXXXX` under the real `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}` of the test host. Bats does not set TMPDIR by default (it uses BATS_TMPDIR for its own files), so unless the suite's setup exports TMPDIR into the case directory, the publish tests touch the shared system temp directory and, on a killed test run, leave the two files described in DISS-R3-002 behind. The stub's python branch is correctly single-quoted and runs with `-I`; the fixtures are literal public text; nothing else leaks out of the case tree.
findings.failure_mode: Test runs write transient files to the host's shared temp directory rather than the isolated case directory, and an interrupted run leaves them there.
findings.suggested_fix: In the bats `setup` (or in the `publish` helper), `export TMPDIR="$CASE_DIR/tmp"; mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"` so the orchestrator's mktemp calls land under the case tree and are removed with it. Optionally assert at the end of the bug-283 cases that `$TMPDIR` is empty, which also pins the helper's cleanup.
findings.failure_scenario: Test runs write transient files to the host's shared temp directory rather than the isolated case directory, and an interrupted run leaves them there.
